chapter_title: Bharat Our Land (How I Taught My Grandmother to Read)
subject: English

Period schedule:

Total: 5 periods · 4h 10min

periods.activity_title: Entering the Ode — Reading and First Appreciation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reflect and Respond (p.23): National Anthem table — states, mountain ranges, rivers.
Reflect and Respond (p.23): paired discussion on what 'Jaya he' conveys.
Reading for Appreciation (p.23): odd-one-out for four underlined words.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the poem aloud expressively while students follow in their textbooks (p.23–24). Attention is drawn to the refrain, the hyphen pauses, and the three-stanza movement.

Reflect and Respond — students individually complete the National Anthem table (states, mountain ranges, rivers), then share findings. Brief paired exchange on what 'Jaya he' conveys, with two or three pairs reporting aloud.
Reading for Appreciation — teacher reads each underlined word aloud; students choose the odd one out from the three given alternatives for all four items and justify each choice briefly.

Whole-class consolidation: teacher charts the correct odd-one-out answers, draws attention to how each chosen word departs in meaning from the poem's usage, and closes by inviting one student to re-read the first stanza aloud.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem is a translated patriotic ode by Subramania Bharati; alerting students to its Tamil origin enriches their reading from the outset. A common difficulty is distinguishing 'peerless' from 'valuable' — the consolidation band is a good moment to make that semantic distinction explicit. The odd-one-out task on 'auspicious' (fantastic vs. fortunate/favourable) is the trickiest item; pause there for a quick meaning check before moving on.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Check Your Understanding (p.25): mood, tone, rhyme scheme, personification features.
Reading for Appreciation (p.26): match six symbols in Column 1 to what they suggest.
Reading for Appreciation (p.26): select true statements about hyphens' impact.

homework.task_brief: Check Your Understanding (p.25): fill-in-the-blank poem summary using ten box words.

time_bands.activity: Brief re-reading of the full poem by a student volunteer, so the three stanzas are fresh in mind. Teacher names the four features to be completed: mood, tone, rhyme scheme, personification.

Check Your Understanding (p.25) — students complete the four feature boxes individually, then pairs compare. Teacher draws out the contrast between mood (reverential, celebratory) and tone (passionate patriotism) as a key literary distinction.

Symbolism matching (p.26) — teacher presents the two-column table on the board; students work individually to pair each symbol with its suggestion, then the class constructs the correct key together with brief justification for each match.

Hyphen impact task (p.26) — teacher reads each of the five options aloud; students select the true ones and defend their choices. Class identifies options 2 and 4 as false and articulates why the hyphen creates assertion rather than doubt or contrast.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem's parallel hyphen structure — treasure named before the hyphen, rhetorical assertion after — is the defining formal feature students are likely to under-appreciate; the final band focuses their attention precisely here. A common pitfall is conflating personification with apostrophe; when completing the feature table note that apostrophe (India addressed as 'she') is the broader device and personification is embedded within it. The fill-in summary (ten box words) is set as an unhurried independent task for homework so students can revisit the full poem text without time pressure.

periods.activity_title: Close Reading, Allusion, and Suffix Word-Building

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Critical Reflection (p.28): identify three allusions — Upanishads, Brahma-knowledge, Buddha's dhamma.
Critical Reflection (p.28–29): extract questions — Himavant, question marks, Ganga, Upanishads.
Vocabulary in Context (p.29): complete suffix table (-ous, -ity, -est, -less) from poem.

time_bands.activity: Allusion identification (p.28) — teacher explains allusion using the definition box, then guides students to locate all three allusions (Upanishads, Brahma-knowledge, Buddha's dhamma) and articulate what each refers to culturally and philosophically.

Extract-based close reading (p.28–29) — students read the first-stanza extract silently, then answer all five sub-questions: filling the blank on 'mighty', choosing the purpose of the question marks, explaining 'generous' applied to the Ganga, explaining 'graceful', and choosing 'unmatched' for the Upanishads. Answers discussed whole-class.

Vocabulary in Context — suffix table (p.29): teacher reviews the four suffixes (-ous, -ity, -est, -less) with meanings, then students scan the poem to find one word exemplifying each suffix. Pairs share findings; teacher confirms and notes the words on the board before students copy the completed table.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often treat allusion as simple naming; the task here requires them to explain what each reference imports culturally — the philosophical weight of the Upanishads, the non-violence of Buddha's dhamma — so press for that second step. For the extract close-reading, the rhetorical questions (lines 4 and 6 of the extract) are frequently misread as genuine inquiry; the answer 'emphasise a point' should be derived from the poem's celebratory tone rather than memorised. The suffix task grounds vocabulary work in the poem's own language, making 'antiquity' (-ity) the most likely sticking point — pronounce and define it before students search.

periods.activity_title: Listening to Travellers, Speaking about Home

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Listen and Respond (p.30): identify speaker numbers for two pictures (hiker, rock-climber).
Listen and Respond (p.31): match statements to speakers; two statements unused.
Speaking Activity (p.23–32): paired praise of home village/town/city using six cues.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the listening task: four speakers describe their favourite travel destinations in India. Students note their answer sheets and look at the two pictures (hiker, rock-climber) before the first play.

First listening — teacher reads the transcript aloud at a measured pace; students write the speaker number for each picture. Second listening follows immediately; students complete the six-statement matching task, identifying which two statements are unused. Class constructs the answer key aloud.

Bridge: teacher invites students to notice which speaker's landscape connects most directly to imagery in the poem — the Ganga riverside (Speaker 1), the Western Ghats mountains (Speaker 2). Brief whole-class exchange before the speaking task opens.

Speaking Activity — in pairs, students take turns praising their own village, town or city using the six provided cues (p.31). After paired practice, four or five students share with the class; peers listen and express whether they agree or disagree with each choice of asset and give a reason.

periods.teacher_notes: The transcript features four distinct natural landscapes — riverside, mountains, desert, forest — each echoing a different face of the India celebrated in the poem; this connection energises the bridge band. A common listening error is assigning the desert (Speaker 3) to rock-climbing because of its 'adventure' feel; remind students that the photographs show specific activities, not landscapes, so the match depends on activity description. During the speaking activity, insist that agreement or disagreement comes with a stated reason, not just a yes/no — this keeps the exchange analytical rather than merely affirmative.

periods.activity_title: Writing a Memory, Exploring India's Voices

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Writing Task (p.23–32): paragraph about a memorable place visited — five guided prompts.
Learning Beyond the Text (p.23–32): search, share, and explain a patriotic poem or song in a regional language.

homework.task_brief: Vocabulary in Context (p.30): add four suffixes (-tion, -ive, -ment, -ed) to form new words and write a sentence for each.

time_bands.activity: Teacher models the writing task: on the board, notes brief answers to the five guiding questions for a shared example place (e.g. a famous riverbank). Students then plan their own paragraph by jotting one phrase against each prompt before drafting.

Guided writing — students draft their full paragraph independently. Teacher circulates, prompting students who stall on the 'preparation' or 'activities' prompts. Peers exchange drafts for a quick read and offer one specific improvement suggestion; writers make a revision on the spot.

Two or three volunteers read their paragraphs aloud. Class responds to whether the description creates a vivid sense of place and whether the five elements are woven in naturally rather than listed mechanically.

Learning Beyond the Text — students share any patriotic poem or song they know in a regional language (Tamil, Hindi, Marathi, Telugu, etc.), recite or sing a line, and explain its meaning in English. Teacher connects each offering back to the devices in Bharati's poem — refrain, apostrophe, hyperbole — showing how the celebration of India recurs across India's languages.

periods.teacher_notes: The writing task asks for a personal memory paragraph built around five concrete questions; students who try to write a general description without anchoring to those five prompts produce vague prose — keep the prompts visible on the board throughout drafting. Bharati himself wrote in Tamil, so the beyond-text activity is especially resonant here: invite any Tamil-speaking student to share a line from the original if they know one. The suffix word-building task (homework) extends the vocabulary work from the earlier suffix table; it is independent and self-contained, requiring only the textbook.
materials: Students' writing paper or exercise books

items.source_lo: Student analyses poetic devices, symbolism, and allusion in a patriotic ode using a poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Subramania Bharati's ode celebrating India's natural grandeur, spiritual heritage, and civilisational legacy through hyperbole, refrain, allusion, and symbolism.
items.item_stem: In the first stanza of 'Bharat Our Land', the poet makes a claim about each treasure using a hyphen. Which of the following best describes what the hyphen achieves in the line 'The mighty Himavant is ours- / there's no equal anywhere on earth'?

options.label: A
options.text: It introduces a qualification that softens the poet's praise of the Himavant.

options.label: B
options.text: It marks a shift from the natural world to the spiritual world.

options.label: C
options.text: It separates a metaphor from its literal meaning.

options.label: D
options.text: It signals a pause before making an absolute assertion of India's supremacy.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student misreads the hyphen as a hedge rather than as a structural separator that amplifies the assertion.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student conflates punctuation function with figurative language analysis.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student imposes a thematic reading onto a syntactic device without textual support.

items.source_lo: Student analyses poetic devices, symbolism, and allusion in a patriotic ode using a poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Subramania Bharati's ode celebrating India's natural grandeur, spiritual heritage, and civilisational legacy through hyperbole, refrain, allusion, and symbolism.
items.item_stem:
Read the stanza beginning 'The mighty Himavant is ours' on p.23, and then answer the following questions.
1. The refrain 'she's peerless, let's praise her!' recurs across all three stanzas. What effect does this repetition create, and how does it transform the poem from a description into a chant?
2. The poet uses hyperbole ('no equal anywhere on earth') alongside allusion (Upanishads, Buddha's dhamma). Evaluate how these two devices work together to build the poem's central argument about India's greatness.
items.visual_stimulus: Read the poem on p.23–24, beginning “The mighty Himavant is ours-”.

expected_elements: Refrain creates chant-like, communal, elevated tone unifying all stanzas.
Repetition shifts poem from catalogue to collective act of praise.
Hyperbole asserts India's absolute superiority to stir emotional pride.
Allusion anchors exaggeration in specific, culturally recognised heritage.
Together they move reader from admiration to reverence and participatory pride.

items.source_lo: Student matches spoken descriptions of natural landscapes to pictures and statements by listening critically for detail.
items.source_context: Four speakers describing favourite Indian travel destinations — riverside, mountains, desert, and forest.
items.item_stem:
Listen to the four speakers describing their favourite travel destinations. Decide whether each of the following statements about the speakers is true or false.
1. Speaker 1 values the riverside primarily because it offers opportunities for adventure sports.
2. Speaker 3 is drawn to the desert because of its visual beauty and the quality of light.
3. Speaker 4 visits forested areas in order to document biodiversity for an online audience.
4. Speaker 2 finds the mountains appealing mainly for their spiritual tranquillity.

options.text: Speaker 1 values the riverside primarily because it offers opportunities for adventure sports.
Speaker 2 finds the mountains appealing mainly for their spiritual tranquillity.
Speaker 3 is drawn to the desert because of its visual beauty and the quality of light.
Speaker 4 visits forested areas in order to document biodiversity for an online audience.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1 — False: Speaker 1 visits the riverside for reflection, meditation, and inner harmony, not adventure sports. 2 — True: Speaker 3 describes sand dunes, colours before sunset, and play of shadows as matchless, seeking photography opportunities. 3 — True: Speaker 4 is a travel vlogger who shares wonders of nature with an online audience. 4 — False: Speaker 2 is drawn to adventure sports in the mountains, not spiritual tranquillity.

items.source_lo: Student matches spoken descriptions of natural landscapes to pictures and statements by listening critically for detail.
items.source_context: Four speakers describing favourite Indian travel destinations — riverside, mountains, desert, and forest.
items.item_stem: Listen to the four speakers again. Speaker 1 describes the Narmada riverside as a place where 'the gentle flow of the river spoke to my soul.' In two or three sentences, explain what this description tells us about Speaker 1's reason for travelling and how it differs from the motivation Speaker 4 gives for visiting the Sundarbans.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Speaker 1 travels to find inner peace — the river's gentleness supports reflection and meditation, making the journey inward rather than outward. Speaker 4, a travel vlogger, visits the Sundarbans to explore biodiversity and share natural wonders with an online audience, so the motivation is outward, creative, and communicative rather than contemplative.

items.item_stem: Your partner has just described a feature of their place as its greatest asset. Do you agree that this feature deserves to be called 'peerless' — as the poet calls India — or do you think another feature is more worthy of that praise? State your position clearly and give at least two reasons for it.

expected_elements: Takes a clear position — agreement or disagreement — without hedging.
Gives at least two distinct reasons supporting the position.
Connects the word 'peerless' to the specific feature under discussion.
Responds to the partner's content, not to a generic claim.
Uses appropriate register — respectful disagreement or qualified agreement.

expected_elements: Follows notice format — heading, date, body, name of issuing authority.

items.item_stem: Write a letter to the editor of a school magazine arguing that students today spend too little time experiencing India's natural landscapes and therefore cannot truly understand the pride Bharati expresses in his poem. Support your argument with at least two specific examples and suggest one practical step schools could take. Write in approximately 150–180 words.

expected_elements: Uses formal letter-to-editor format with appropriate salutation and sign-off.
States the central argument clearly in the opening paragraph.
Provides at least two specific examples linking landscape experience to patriotic understanding.
Proposes one concrete, actionable step for schools.
Maintains a persuasive, formal register throughout without drifting to informal language.

items.item_stem: Match each suffix in Column A with the word from the poem or its family that carries that suffix in Column B.
items.visual_stimulus:
Column A | Column B
-ous | peerless
-ity | auspicious
-est | antiquity
-less | divinest

items.source_lo: Student identifies and applies suffixes to build new words, drawing examples from a poem's own vocabulary.
items.source_context: Suffix patterns (-ous, -ity, -est, -less, -tion, -ive, -ment, -ed) as found in and extended from the poem's language.
items.item_stem: The poem describes India as 'peerless' (without equal). Using the suffix -less as your model, take the word 'bound' and form the word 'boundless'. Then write one sentence using 'boundless' that describes a feature of India's landscape as Bharati might have — making a strong, admiring claim. Next, take the root word 'sanctify' and add the suffix -ed to form 'sanctified'; write one sentence showing how this word would fit the poem's celebration of India's sages. Both sentences together should show how the -less and -ed suffixes create contrasting effects (absence of limit versus completed, honoured action).

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: An acceptable response forms 'boundless' correctly and uses it in a sentence praising an infinite or limitless quality of India (e.g. its rivers, its wisdom, its skies), then forms 'sanctified' and uses it to describe sages having consecrated or made holy the land — demonstrating that -less signals an ongoing, unlimited quality while -ed signals a completed, reverential act.

items.source_context: Patriotic poems and songs in regional Indian languages shared and explained by students in class.
items.item_stem: Name one patriotic poem or song you know in a regional Indian language (other than English). Write down one line or phrase from it in that language, give its meaning in English, and identify one device it shares with Bharati's 'Bharat Our Land' — such as a refrain, hyperbole, apostrophe, or allusion.

expected_elements: Names a specific patriotic poem or song in a named regional language.
Quotes at least one line or phrase in the original language accurately.
Provides a clear, meaningful English translation of the quoted line.
Identifies one shared device and names it correctly.
Explains briefly how the device functions similarly in both texts.

items.source_lo: Student explores patriotic poetry across India's regional languages and explains meaning through multilingual comparison.
items.source_context: Patriotic poems and songs in regional Indian languages shared and explained by students in class.
items.item_stem: Design an outline for a class project that compares how two different regional-language patriotic poems celebrate India. Your outline must include: (a) the titles and languages of the two poems you would study; (b) three specific points of comparison (for example: imagery used, devices employed, aspects of India celebrated); (c) one way in which the project would be presented to the class (poster, oral presentation, written report, or another form). Explain in three to five sentences why comparing poems across languages deepens our understanding of India's cultural identity.

expected_elements: Names two distinct regional-language patriotic poems with their languages.
Identifies three substantive, specific points of comparison.
Proposes a clearly described mode of presentation.
Explains how multilingual comparison reveals shared or divergent cultural values.
Shows awareness that India's identity is expressed through many linguistic traditions.
